references.text: Moses prophesied about a prophet like himself whom the Lord would raise up. Jesus is described in Luke 24:19 precisely as 'a prophet, mighty in deed and word,' which points back to the promise in Deuteronomy 18:15-18 concerning the coming prophet.

The people exclaimed 'a great prophet has arisen among us' after Jesus raised the widow's son in Nain. This confirms the view of Jesus as a prophet mighty in deed, just as the disciples describe him in Luke 24:19. See Luke 7:16.
The Samaritan woman recognizes Jesus as a prophet in John 4:19, which aligns with the description in Luke 24:19 where the disciples call him 'a prophet, mighty in deed and word.'

After the feeding miracle, the people said, 'This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world' (John 6:14). Jesus was recognized as the prophet because of his mighty deeds, as described in Luke 24:19.
Peter speaks of 'Jesus of Nazareth, a man accredited by God to you by miracles, wonders and signs' (Acts 2:22). This is a close parallel to the description in Luke 24:19 of Jesus as mighty in deed.
Stephen refers to Moses as 'mighty in words and deeds' (Acts 7:22), using exactly the same expression applied to Jesus in Luke 24:19. Jesus is the new Moses-figure, the promised prophet.

Jesus revealed himself as a prophet in the Nazareth synagogue by reading from Isaiah and declaring its fulfillment (Luke 4:16-21). He is called 'Jesus of Nazareth' in Luke 24:19, which connects back to this event.
Peter quotes the prophecy from Deuteronomy 18:15 and applies it directly to Jesus in Acts 3:22-23, confirming that Jesus is the prophet Moses foretold—mighty in deed and word.
Jesus himself says 'a prophet cannot perish outside Jerusalem' (Luke 13:33). In Luke 24:19, Jesus is described precisely as a prophet, and the context concerns what happened to him in Jerusalem.
The crowd called Jesus 'the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee' (Matthew 21:11) when he entered Jerusalem. This matches the disciples' description in Luke 24:19 of 'Jesus of Nazareth' as a prophet.
